title: Mary's song (Luke 1:46–55)
hook: she sings of a God who lifts the lowly and sends the rich away empty

segments.voice: Yesterday, two pregnant women, the Visitation: Mary at Elizabeth's door, and a baby who leaped. Your line was: joy knows joy. Did you reach the person who'd understand? Day thirty-nine.

We're still in Elizabeth's house, in the hills. Elizabeth has just cried out a blessing over Mary, and you might expect Mary to say something modest. Thank you. I don't know what's happening either. Instead, Luke gives her a song. Ten verses. And it isn't a lullaby. It starts with thanks, turns to her own small life, and then, without warning, it turns the whole world over. Thrones emptied. Hungry people fed. Rich people walking away with nothing. A young woman from a small village, pregnant and not yet married, singing about the powerful coming down. Churches have sung her song at daily prayer for many centuries. Today's word is its first word.
screen: `STILL IN ELIZABETH'S HOUSE.` → `NOT MODEST. A SONG.` → `THE WORLD TURNED OVER.`

segments.voice: In the King James Bible it begins: "My soul doth magnify the Lord, And my spirit hath rejoiced in God my Saviour." In the old Latin Bible, the first word is Magnificat, magnifies, and that's what the song is called. To magnify is to make bigger. Not to make God bigger than God is, but to make God big in your own eyes, the way a magnifying glass makes something small easy to see. Then Mary looks at herself. She says God has noticed the low estate of his servant girl, and that from now on every generation will call her blessed. And then the song turns outward. "He hath put down the mighty from their seats, and exalted them of low degree. He hath filled the hungry with good things; and the rich he hath sent empty away." Notice the tense. She sings as if it has already happened, the way the Hebrew prophets sometimes spoke of what they were sure was coming. And it echoes an older song. In the book of Samuel, a woman named Hannah, who also waited for a child, sings something very close: God raises the poor from the dust. Mary is singing in her people's words, in the line of the women before her. Churches keep her song in different ways. Catholics sing it at evening prayer, and Anglicans at Evensong; Lutherans sing it at vespers. Orthodox Christians sing it in the morning service, with a hymn honoring Mary between the verses. Catholics and Orthodox hear it as the song of the Mother of God; many Protestants hear it as a model of praise, and a warning to anyone comfortable. All of them sing the same promise. The lowly are lifted.
screen: `MY SOUL DOTH MAGNIFY THE LORD.` · `SHE SINGS AS IF IT'S DONE.` · `HANNAH SANG IT FIRST.` · `SUNG AT EVENING AND MORNING PRAYER.` · then, large: `THE LOWLY ARE LIFTED.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice. Sit, and take a slow breath. Mary's song starts with thanks. So think back over the last few days and find one thing to be grateful for. A small one is fine. Someone who made room for you. A meal. A morning that went right. Now put it into one line of your own words. Not a poem. Just a sentence you'd actually say. If you have a pen or your phone, write it down. If you pray, you can offer the line as thanks. If you don't, just let it be true. Two minutes. The bell holds the time.
Magnificat. Latin for magnifies: the first word of Mary's song, where the mighty come down and the lowly are lifted.
Your line: the lowly are lifted. Keep your line of thanks with you today, and notice one person who's usually overlooked. Lift them a little. Day thirty-nine.

howItsDone: The Magnificat is sung or said every evening in Catholic vespers and in Anglican Evening Prayer, and at Lutheran vespers; Orthodox churches sing it at the morning service, with a hymn to Mary as a refrain.

fork.setup: you're Mary. your older relative has just blessed you at her door. what comes out of your mouth?
options: a quiet thank you, and a question about what happens next.
a song about God lifting the lowly and emptying thrones.
a worried list of what people back home will say.
fork.reveal: she sings: my soul doth magnify the Lord. and the song ends with the mighty put down and the hungry filled.

original.note: Greek: makes great, magnifies. the first word of Mary's song in Luke's Greek; Latin made it magnificat.

trapdoor: what you thought: a gentle hymn about Mary.
what it means: a song of thanks that turns into a promise: the mighty come down, the lowly are lifted, the hungry are fed.
what a scholar hears: it's woven from older Hebrew songs, above all Hannah's in 1 Samuel 2. and a few old Latin manuscripts even give the song to Elizabeth instead of Mary.

notes: 'The longest speech any woman makes in the New Testament' is a common claim; confirm or soften.
'Sung almost every evening for well over a thousand years' rests on the Magnificat's place at vespers in the Western daily office (Rule of Benedict era onward); confirm.
Orthodox use: the Magnificat sung at Matins with the refrain 'More honorable than the cherubim'; confirm wording 'a hymn honoring Mary between the verses'.
Trapdoor: a few Old Latin manuscripts (and some patristic citations) read 'Elisabeth' at Luke 1:46; confirm the Keeper wants this detail.
Carry practice ('lift them a little') expands the outline's line of thanks with the day's line; confirm.
